title: Little whistle. Big voice.
dek: At a Columbus workbench, that familiar sound starts with a flat piece of brass.
coverAlt: Illustrated brass pea whistle, navy cord and metal blank on a workbench
intro: You know the sound before you see the thing making it. A game pauses, someone turns, and there it is: a little whistle. At American Whistle Corporation in Columbus, brass is cut, shaped, assembled, and tested until it can do that small but very noticeable job. Inside, its design makes the clear sound possible.

sections.title: Start with a flat sheet
paragraphs: Start with the brass sheet or coil. It looks very different from the curved whistle in your hand, doesn’t it? A stamping press cuts blanks for the body and mouthpiece. Forming operations then bend them into shape. The company’s account of the process puts careful tooling right at the beginning: each part has to fit the work that comes next.

Now look along a finished whistle’s seam, opening, and ring attachment. There’s a reason for each of them. The brass has to accept those precise shapes and stand up to outdoor use. I like this part of the story: an object that looks so familiar becomes easier to appreciate once you can imagine it lying flat on a workbench.

sections.title: The pea has room to move
paragraphs: Hear that trill? A little moving part helps make it. In a pea whistle, a small sphere sits inside the chamber. Air enters through the mouthpiece and passes the opening; the moving pea changes the sound. The size and space around it matter. It needs room to move, even though the whole whistle fits easily in your palm.

American Whistle describes inserting the pea by hand and joining the mouthpiece carefully around the air passage. Follow that path from the entrance to the chamber. It’s a small space with a lot to do. A shiny finish catches your eye, but the shapes underneath are what make the sound work.

sections.title: One last listen
paragraphs: And now, someone listens. The company says every finished whistle is sound-tested by hand. Looking at the brass tells you some things; hearing the assembled whistle tells you something else. All the cutting, forming, and joining ends with a person checking the result. Ooh, there’s our familiar signal again.

The Columbus business traces its production back to 1956. If you’d like to see more than the finished object, its website has factory-tour information. Check the current arrangements before planning a visit. For now, you can follow its published process and look again at the whistle’s tiny working parts. There’s plenty to notice without taking one apart.

aside.title: That little rattle has a job
aside.text: The pea moves inside the chamber. Next time you hear the trill, you’ll know there’s something busy happening in that tiny space. Neat, right?

practical.label: Look closely
practical.text: Find the mouthpiece, sound opening, body seam, and lanyard ring on a metal whistle.

practical.label: Plan ahead
practical.text: Use the company's tour page for current booking details and access rules.

signoff: A small piece of brass, a lot of careful work, and one very familiar sound. ♡

title: A little clay. A lot of hands.
dek: Let’s follow a piece of Rookwood pottery through the work that gives it a place in someone’s home.
coverAlt: Illustrated green pottery vase, clay bowl and shaping tool in a workshop
intro: Pick a vase you like and look past the color for a moment. Someone chose that curve. Someone worked on the surface. Other hands helped it reach the shelf. At Cincinnati’s Rookwood Pottery, those decisions are part of a story that began in 1880. The finished piece is only our first clue.

sections.title: Art for the room you live in
paragraphs: Maria Longworth Nichols Storer founded Rookwood in Cincinnati in 1880. The pottery’s history begins with a former schoolhouse, Ohio River clay, and a single kiln. Imagine starting there, with a material that can become a cup, a tile, or something made simply because you want to see its shape. It’s an inviting place to begin a making story.

Rookwood’s early artists developed individual designs and worked with form, decoration, and glaze. So when you look at a piece, try following one choice at a time. The outline first. Then the surface. Then where the glaze changes in the light. There’s no need to know all the pottery terms before you can notice something you like.

sections.title: A piece passes from hand to hand
paragraphs: Ready for the part that surprised me in Rookwood’s own description? A piece passes through at least thirteen sets of hands. Shaping, finishing, glazing, and firing call for different kinds of attention. Clay also changes while it dries and fires. The work has pauses in it; a fresh form can’t be rushed straight to the table.

A tile asks us to step back a little. Rookwood still makes architectural tile and custom work, so one small surface might become part of an entire room. Look at how neighboring pieces repeat a color or pattern. With a vase, you can walk around the object. With a tiled wall, the object is all around you.

sections.title: Look across time, then look again
paragraphs: To see how those choices change over time, look through museum collections and Rookwood’s own history. Compare an older piece with something made today. You might notice a familiar approach to color or a completely different shape. Let one detail catch your attention before reading its label; then see what the maker or museum can tell you about it.

If you’re planning a Cincinnati visit, use Rookwood’s current information for shop hours and any factory-tour arrangements. A shop visit and a look at a collection are different ways to meet the work. Choose the one that fits your day. Either way, give the small objects time. A cup can hold a surprisingly long conversation.

aside.title: Try looking twice
aside.text: First the shape, then the glaze. Does the piece feel different when you pay attention to just one of those? I’d love to know which detail you noticed first.

practical.label: At the museum
practical.text: Search the Cincinnati Art Museum collection for Rookwood objects before a visit.

practical.label: At the maker
practical.text: Check Rookwood's current workshop and tour listings for booking details.

signoff: Next time you pick up a favorite cup, spare a thought for the hands that got it to you. ♡

title: Ooh, look at that glass.
dek: In Toledo, light, heat, and a maker’s timing turn something familiar into something worth stopping for.
coverAlt: Painted blue-green glass vase and amber bowl with a studio furnace behind
intro: Move a little to the side. See how the light changes? Glass is lovely company for a curious eye, and Toledo gives us plenty to look at. We’ll start with the city’s glass story, spend time with the objects at the museum, and see how today’s studio programs can bring the making a little closer. No need to hurry past the windows.

sections.title: The building joins the lesson
paragraphs: Toledo’s connection with glass includes both industry and art. The city’s manufacturing history helps explain why glass belongs in its story, while the Toledo Museum of Art invites you to consider what artists can do with it. Keep both in mind. The same material can be part of an ordinary day and the thing that makes you stop in a gallery.

The museum’s Glass Pavilion gives the collection a building with glass at the center of its design. Look at the works, then look at the room around them. Reflections and transparency make the edges interesting. We can take a slow lap and let different surfaces catch the light instead of choosing a favorite immediately.

sections.title: A workshop opened the door
paragraphs: There’s an important studio chapter here too. Workshops at the Toledo Museum of Art in 1962 helped establish the American studio glass movement. Artists explored working with glass on a scale that opened up new possibilities outside conventional industrial production. That’s a useful thought to carry into the collection: who gets to work with a material, and what can they try?

Start with an object that holds your attention. Notice its thickness, color, bubbles, or the way a rim bends the light. The museum label can help with the technique, but your eyes can begin the conversation. Two pieces made from glass may feel completely different. That’s part of the pleasure of staying awhile.

sections.title: Now, watch the making
paragraphs: Watching the work gives those finished surfaces another meaning. The museum offers glass demonstrations and classes through its studio programs. Check the current schedule before making that the center of your visit; a gallery day and a booked class ask for different plans. If a demonstration fits, settle in and watch how the maker handles the changing material.

A class is a chance to follow the studio’s instruction and discover how much attention a small object asks for. If you’d rather just look, the collection rewards a slow visit. We can leave with one favorite color, one curious shape, or a question for another visit. You don’t have to make a vase to start noticing glass.

aside.title: A different view
aside.text: Try looking from another angle without touching the work. A reflection can move, an edge can catch the light, and suddenly you’re noticing something else.

practical.label: Before you go
practical.text: Check the museum's current Glass Pavilion access and demonstration calendar.

practical.label: In the gallery
practical.text: Compare the methods listed for two different glass objects.

signoff: Now even the glass on an ordinary windowsill might get a second look. ♡

title: There’s a story in these tires.
dek: Let’s follow Akron’s rubber history from a familiar wheel back to the people and experiments behind it.
coverAlt: Illustration of a rubber tire beside a workshop bench and a sheet of rubber
intro: We pass tires every day. Usually we only notice them when something goes wrong. Give this one a moment instead: the tread, the curved side, the material that has to meet the road again and again. Akron’s history can make that ordinary object much more interesting. That work helped shape a city.

sections.title: Before the automobile took over
paragraphs: Let’s go back to 1898. Goodyear began in Akron with products including bicycle and carriage tires, horseshoe pads, and poker chips. A rather different shelf from the one you might expect, right? Cars would make tires a much bigger part of the story. Those early objects are a good reminder that rubber already had plenty to do before the automobile became an everyday sight.

The company took its name from Charles Goodyear, whose work with heat and sulfur helped turn natural rubber into a more useful, durable material. The process is called vulcanization. You can begin with the things it made possible: a flexible tire, a hard-wearing pad, an object that holds its shape while doing its job. A material change can reach into an ordinary day in surprising ways.

sections.title: An everyday material, a lot to learn
paragraphs: Now back to the tire. It needs to do several jobs at once, carrying a load while meeting a changing road. The history of rubber and tire making is full of attempts to improve familiar things. Akron’s industrial story carries forward into research on polymers, the broader family of materials that includes many substances we encounter every day.

In 1909, Buchtel College, now the University of Akron, began teaching rubber chemistry. That connection between local work and study grew into a much wider polymer research story. You don’t need a chemistry degree to start noticing the questions. For a tire, think about wear, flexibility, and contact with the road. There is a lot of testing behind a shape we barely glance at in a parking lot.

sections.title: Meet the city around the work
paragraphs: Now look beyond the factory. Goodyear Heights began as a planned neighborhood for workers and their families. Its streets and houses give the industrial story another scale: home, school, a walk through the neighborhood. Local labor histories add the working conditions, organizing, and difficult changes behind the company timelines. I’d make room for both accounts. They introduce us to different sides of the same city.

If you visit a museum or attend a public program, check its own current visitor information. Research buildings and working factories have different access arrangements. We can follow the history through places that welcome visitors, and keep the next ordinary tire in mind as we go. It has a much longer story now, hasn’t it?

aside.title: Start with the tread
aside.text: Look at a stationary tire’s pattern, then ask what its material needs to withstand. That small question is a good doorway into Akron’s much bigger story.

practical.label: For context
practical.text: Read a local labor history alongside a company timeline.

practical.label: On a map
practical.text: Locate Market Street and Goodyear Heights to see how production and housing related.

signoff: An everyday object can introduce you to a whole city. Akron is a good place to begin. ♡

title: Pull up a chair. Let’s order chili.
dek: Spaghetti, a spiced sauce, and that generous pile of cheese. I’ll help you make sense of the menu.
coverAlt: Painted plate of Cincinnati chili with spaghetti and shredded cheddar in a diner
intro: First Cincinnati chili order? The numbers on the menu will make sense in a minute. A three-way brings spaghetti, chili, and shredded cheese together on the plate; from there, you choose what else sounds good. We can learn a little of the parlor’s history while you decide. Lunch should still get most of our attention. ♡

sections.title: From a theater-side shop
paragraphs: The story takes us back to 1922. Macedonian immigrant brothers Tom and John Kiradjieff began selling their seasoned meat sauce near Cincinnati’s Empress Theatre. Empress Chili’s account remembers theater patrons and performers among the early customers. Picture the kind of meal that fits around a night out: something quick, familiar, and worth coming back for.

Cincinnati chili is served as a spiced meat sauce over spaghetti or on a hot dog. That helps explain why the plate looks different from the bowl you might have imagined. Parlors have their own recipes and regulars. We’ll start with the common menu terms, then leave you room to find the version you like.

sections.title: The numbers are your guide
paragraphs: Here’s your little menu key. A three-way is spaghetti, chili, and cheese. A four-way adds onions or beans; a five-way adds both. Want the sauce on a hot dog? Look for a coney, with cheese and other toppings according to the parlor’s menu. There, much less mysterious already.

If you’re ordering a four-way, just say whether you want the onions or the beans. You don’t have to pretend you’ve been coming here forever. Check the portion choices too; a smaller order can be a nice introduction. Once it arrives, take a look at the fine sauce and the spaghetti underneath before the cheese disappears into your first bite.

sections.title: The parlor is part of the dish
paragraphs: Take a moment with the room around your plate. Cincinnati’s chili story belongs to counters, quick meals, and family-run parlors as well as recipes. Local food histories trace those connections to theater crowds and everyday eating. A place that becomes someone’s usual lunch stop has a different kind of importance from a dish you only try on holiday.

So let this first visit be a beginning. Read the parlor’s own story, look at the menu, and decide what you’d order another time. You might be curious about a coney next, or about how a different place seasons its sauce. We have plenty of room for another lunch. For this one, go on—your plate is waiting.

aside.title: Three, four, or five?
aside.text: Spaghetti + chili + cheese gets you to three. Onions or beans make four; both make five. You’ve got it. Now choose what sounds good.

practical.label: Order plainly
practical.text: Name the toppings you want, especially when ordering a four-way.

practical.label: Choose your parlor
practical.text: Check a restaurant's own current menu and location details before visiting.

signoff: Save your favorite order. Next time, you can show me what you picked. ♡

title: Save room for a buckeye.
dek: A little peanut butter, a little chocolate, and one bare patch that gives the sweet its Ohio name.
coverAlt: Illustrated buckeye candies with uncovered peanut-butter tops on a navy plate
intro: I saved the sweet part for you. See the little pale circle at the top? That’s what makes this chocolate-dipped peanut-butter candy look like a buckeye nut. It’s a familiar Ohio treat with a tiny detail worth noticing before the first bite. Let’s start with the tree, then head to the kitchen. ♡

sections.title: First, the actual buckeye
paragraphs: The Ohio buckeye is the state tree. Its shiny brown nut has a lighter patch, a shape that’s easy to recognize once someone points it out. Look at a picture of the nut beside the candy and you’ll see the connection immediately. The cook leaves part of the peanut-butter center uncovered to keep that resemblance.

The nut itself isn’t the dessert; the candy is made from peanut butter and chocolate. Keep the two separate when showing someone the name. You can appreciate the tree’s place in Ohio’s symbols, then enjoy the edible version at the table. It’s a small introduction to the state that doesn’t take a whole history lesson.

sections.title: A recipe that traveled
paragraphs: The candy has a kitchen story too. Experience Columbus credits Gail Tabor with the familiar recipe in the 1960s, while Ohio State alumni material shows it circulating among readers by the early 1970s. Recipes travel from one household to another. By the time a batch reaches your table, the person making it may have learned it from someone close to them.

The recognizable step is the dip: lower the peanut-butter center into chocolate and keep a little patch bare. Recipes can vary in proportions, size, and texture, but that last detail keeps the name visible. If you’re watching someone make a batch, this is the moment to look. Ooh, there it is—one little sweet becoming a buckeye.

sections.title: More than game day
paragraphs: A box of buckeyes fits into more than a game-day gathering. They turn up as gifts and on holiday tables too. The shape gives you something to share besides chocolate: someone asks about the uncovered top, and now you have a story to tell. No special occasion needed. A neighbor and a plate are a perfectly good start.

If you’re making a batch, enjoy the part where the shapes come together. Rolling and dipping gives each one a slightly different outline. Keep a little space on the plate for the uneven ones, too. The small pale circle at the top does the important work: one glance, and the buckeye shape is unmistakable.

aside.title: Leave that little circle
aside.text: Cover the whole center in chocolate and you hide the detail that gives the candy its name. Funny how the smallest part can tell the whole story.

practical.label: Spot the detail
practical.text: Look for the small circle of peanut butter left visible above the chocolate.

practical.label: Share the story
practical.text: Show someone a photo of the tree's nut beside the candy to explain its name.

signoff: One for you, one to share. We can tell the tree story between bites. ♡

title: A market full of good things.
dek: Cleveland’s West Side Market has a beautiful ceiling. The people at the counters deserve your attention too.
coverAlt: Painted vaulted market hall with food counters and a sunlit aisle
intro: Look up first. That tiled vault is quite an entrance, isn’t it? Now look down at the counters. Cleveland’s West Side Market has served shoppers since 1912, and the day’s food still draws people through the doors. Let’s take a lap before we choose anything. I’m curious what will end up on your table.

sections.title: A public place since 1912
paragraphs: The present building opened on November 2, 1912, following the earlier Pearl Street market nearby. Its clock tower, tiled vault, and rows of stands belong to a city that once had three public markets. West Side Market is the one that remains. Spend a moment with the architecture, then follow the movement of people doing their shopping.

The market’s history includes immigrant communities and vendors from many backgrounds. Cleveland Historical and the market’s own tour give names and context to some of those stories. Keep them nearby if a detail makes you curious. A building can tell you when it opened; the people who used it help explain why it stayed part of the neighborhood.

sections.title: Let the counters shape the meal
paragraphs: Let’s think about a meal. The market lists produce, meat, seafood, cheese, baked goods, and prepared food among its offerings. You could start with bread and a few ingredients for dinner, or choose something ready to eat. Take a look at several counters before deciding. There’s room to change the plan when something catches your eye.

Each vendor is an independent business. Ask a question when the counter is ready for you, and leave space for people doing their regular shopping. If you want a photograph of a stall, ask first. The best way to enjoy this place is to share the aisles comfortably with the people who use them every week.

sections.title: Carry the market back to your table
paragraphs: By the time you leave, you may have a lunch, a bag of ingredients, or just a better idea of what you want to cook. The market’s original mix of indoor food stands and produce sellers suggests the same pleasure: different counters contributing to one table. Remember which stall helped you choose something. That’s a good detail to carry home.

Use the market’s current website for opening hours, vendor information, and building updates. If a particular business is the reason for your visit, check its details too. Then give yourself enough time to browse. We’ve looked at the ceiling, met a few counters, and found something to eat. A pretty good way to spend a piece of Cleveland.

aside.title: What are we making for dinner?
aside.text: Pick one ingredient that looks good, then see what the other stalls can add. A market is a lovely place to let dinner change its mind.

practical.label: Make a plan
practical.text: Choose a meal before you browse, then let the available stalls change the details.

practical.label: Check first
practical.text: Use the market's official site for current hours, vendors, and construction updates.

signoff: Got everything? Good. Let’s see what that market bag becomes at the table. ♡

title: A book, a window, an afternoon.
dek: At Columbus Main Library, follow an old city map or settle in for one more chapter.
coverAlt: Illustrated library reading table and open book beside a window overlooking greenery
intro: You don’t have to fill every hour of a day out. At Columbus Main Library, choose what feels right. A book by the window? A question about an old house? A little time with the city’s records? The building opened in 1907, but there are plenty of reasons to spend an ordinary afternoon here now.

sections.title: A building for readers and neighbors
paragraphs: A Carnegie gift helped fund the Main Library’s original building. Later changes opened its spaces toward nearby Topiary Park, adding a different kind of welcome to the old address. The library describes an atrium, children’s area, meeting and study spaces, and a reading room facing the green. Let’s start by finding a place where you’d like to sit.

Around you, people may be doing quite different things: browsing, working, helping a child choose a book, or asking a question. A public library makes room for those days to overlap. You can join in with something as simple as reading a chapter. I’m happy to let the next stop wait a little.

sections.title: The city is in its files
paragraphs: If you’ve brought a question, Local History & Genealogy is a good place to take it. The library’s house-research guide points to city directories going back to 1841 and historic maps. Start with an address or a family name, then ask which records might help. An ordinary street can become much more interesting when you see an earlier version of it.

Research help is available through the library, including its reserve-an-expert service. You don’t need to know the right archival words before asking. A directory might give you a name; a map might show the shape of a building. Some questions stay open. Follow what the records actually show and keep the next question ready.

sections.title: Walk back into the neighborhood
paragraphs: When you’re ready to stretch your legs, Kaufman Plaza connects the library with Topiary Park. Step outside for a little green, then look back toward the building. The reading afternoon and the neighborhood belong together. A quiet place indoors can be part of getting to know a city, just as much as a busy street.

Before you go, check the library’s hours and any booking required for a program, room, or research appointment. You can keep the rest of the visit loose. Read, ask, wander out to the park. There’s something nice about leaving with a question you didn’t arrive with—and perhaps a title to look for another day.

aside.title: Bring one small question
aside.text: An address, a family name, a street you keep passing. That’s enough to start a conversation with the local history collection.

practical.label: Start inside
practical.text: Ask staff where to find the reading room or Local History & Genealogy resources.

practical.label: Check the day
practical.text: Confirm current hours and any program registration on the library site.

signoff: One more page? Of course. I said we had time. ♡

title: Let’s see what’s growing.
dek: At Dayton’s Possum Creek, garden plots change throughout the growing season.
coverAlt: Painted garden beds, tomato plants and watering can beside a quiet path in evening light
intro: A garden looks different from one month to the next. That’s what I’d like you to notice at Possum Creek MetroPark in Dayton. The community plots have people caring for them through a whole growing season: planting, watering, weeding, and finding out what the weather has decided. Let’s look at the small routines that keep a shared garden going.

sections.title: A marked piece of shared ground
paragraphs: Start with the edges of a plot. Five Rivers MetroParks’ rules mark out each gardener’s space, shared paths, and seasonal water access. A clear boundary sounds simple, but it gives everyone room to work. You can tend your own patch while leaving the next gardener a path to theirs. Little practical choices make a shared place easier to use.

Possum Creek’s gardens sit in a wider park landscape with farm activities and opportunities to learn outdoors. A rented plot has its own caretaker within that public setting. If you’re visiting, enjoy the areas open to visitors and leave the beds to their gardeners. We can be interested in what’s growing without stepping into someone’s work.

sections.title: The season asks you to return
paragraphs: Planting day is only the beginning. Water, weeds, pests, and the end of a plant’s season all ask someone to return. MetroParks specifies organic practices and sets out responsibilities for common paths and water. Before taking a plot, read those details and think about the weeks ahead. The work is easier to picture when you imagine more than the first sunny afternoon.

A month from now, notice what has changed from the public paths. Plants grow at different rates; weather changes the week’s jobs. A garden doesn’t have to produce a perfect basket to show how much attention it receives. Sometimes the interesting thing is a newly cleared row or a gardener making room for the next planting.

sections.title: Growing beside other people
paragraphs: Interested in a plot yourself? The garden uses seasonal registration. Ask Five Rivers MetroParks about current availability and rules before making plans. Think about how often you can return and what you’d like to learn. There’s no need to promise a whole season of care before you’ve understood what taking a plot involves.

And if you’re here for a park visit, that belongs in the story too. Follow the visitor guidance, respect the marked beds, and notice how this part of the park is shaped by repeated work. Someone returned to water. Someone cleared a path. The next time you pass, the ground will have a little more of the season to reveal.

aside.title: A little room for the neighbors
aside.text: The paths and water are shared, even when the plots have different caretakers. Leaving room for the next person is part of growing things here.

practical.label: To garden
practical.text: Check Five Rivers MetroParks' current registration and rules before planning for a plot.

practical.label: To visit
practical.text: Use the park's visitor information and respect marked garden boundaries.

signoff: Shall we see how it looks another month? Gardens are good at giving us a reason to return. ♡

title: Got a little time? Let’s walk through Athens.
dek: From Ohio University’s College Green to Uptown, a few ordinary blocks hold plenty of stories.
coverAlt: Painted college green with a tree-lined path and red brick academic building
intro: Let’s start at College Green. You can look at the old buildings, but watch the paths too: they’re part of somebody’s walk to class, a meeting, or the library. Ohio University and Uptown Athens sit close enough for us to meet both on foot. We’ll take the public paths, leave people room to get on with their day, and see where a little wandering leads.

sections.title: Through the gateway
paragraphs: The Alumni Gateway is a nice place to begin. Ohio University describes a tradition of entering through it as a new student and leaving after commencement. Today, it also does an ordinary, useful thing: connects campus with town. Stand back for a moment and look in both directions. We can follow the green first and leave Uptown for later.

Cutler Hall is the oldest building on College Green. Over its long history it has held different university uses, including classrooms and a library. That’s something to keep in mind while you look at the facade. A historic building has had many ordinary mornings. Its place in the university comes from all those days as well as the big occasions.

sections.title: A working campus, not a still picture
paragraphs: The university’s suggested visitor route includes College Green, Alden Library, and places for study, food, and recreation. Baker University Center is a meeting point between classes and activities. You start to see the shape of a student day in those stops: somewhere to read, somewhere to eat, someone to meet before moving on.

This is an active campus, so use public paths and the university’s visitor guidance. A booked admissions tour is the way to see the spaces included in that program. We can enjoy the green without treating every doorway as an invitation. Take a seat if you like. Sometimes staying still for a minute tells you more than hurrying to the next building.

sections.title: Out to Athens
paragraphs: Ready for the town side? Head toward Court Street and Uptown. Ohio University’s introduction to Athens points to food, music, and arts as part of the relationship between campus and community. Choose a public street, look at the businesses, and let something catch your interest. There are neighbors and working days here beyond the university calendar.

Before heading back, turn around and look toward the gateway again. We’ve only crossed a few blocks, but they connect different parts of Athens: the green, classrooms, shops, and places to meet. If you’re planning a more formal campus visit, check the university’s current tour information. For a simple walk, leave yourself enough time to notice both sides.

aside.title: Try the view both ways
aside.text: Toward the green, then back toward Uptown. The gateway is a good reminder that a campus day is also a day in somebody’s town.

practical.label: For a campus visit
practical.text: Use Ohio University's current admissions tour information for guided access.
